summary: The video quantitatively evaluates common trading psychology rules—such as stopping after consecutive losses, taking profits early, revenge trading, and skipping trades—by modeling a baseline profitable trader across 10,000 simulated trading years using Claude. The findings demonstrate that for an already profitable trader, behavioral rules that artificially truncate trading volume (such as daily profit targets or hesitation after losses) consistently reduce expected annual returns, while selective position sizing on high-conviction setups adds substantial value. For losing traders, however, any rule that reduces trade volume reduces losses. The video concludes with four copy-paste Claude prompts allowing traders to test these concepts and check their own trade histories for streakiness and tail risk.

key_points: The presenter pulled 83 common trading psychology concepts and tested them across 10,000 simulated trading years using Claude.
The rules fall into three categories: concepts that work and add significant money, concepts that do not work at all, and nuanced concepts dependent on individual edge and execution.
Presenter background: Studied Math and Economics at UCLA, worked over 3 years in investment banking, and spent the last 2 years building trading systems.
Trading psychology concepts cannot be tested directly as feelings (tilt, fear, greed), but can be tested as actions: standing down, sizing down, skipping, or stopping.
The simulation is strategy-agnostic: rules are tested against an assumed baseline profitable trader edge rather than technical indicators.
Baseline trader parameters: 37% win rate, risking $500 per trade, average winner +$1,000 (2R), average loser -$500 (-1R), expected value +$50 per trade.
Account parameters: $50,000 starting account, 750 trades per year (approximately 3 trades per day).
Simulation scope: Monte Carlo simulation of 10,000 versions of that year run using Claude.
Introduces 'streakiness' (autocorrelation of outcomes): whether a loss makes the next trade more likely to lose.

segments.topic: Dash 1: A Single Trade Means Nothing & Sample Size
key_points: 93.5% of simulated years contain a run of 10 losses in a row for the baseline trader (median longest losing streak in a year is 12 in a row).
A coin-flip trader (no edge) hits a 10-loss streak 99% of years; an expert trader (3.5x better than baseline) still hits a 10-loss streak 54% of years.
Even after 100 trades, there is a 24.5% chance that a truly profitable strategy shows a net loss.
Statistically, approximately 809 trades are required for a measured edge to converge near the true edge within a 95% confidence band.

segments.topic: Dash 2: Revenge Trading / Chasing Money Back
key_points: Normal baseline trader median account after a year: $97,830.
Doubling size after every loss (revenge trading / Martingale) yields a median account of $157,834, because average position size increases by 3.5x.
However, doubling after a loss adds +2.1 percentage points (pp) extra chance of halving the account compared to random sizing up.
Without position size caps, 99.9% of simulated revenge trading accounts go broke (-$57,830 drawdown beyond initial capital).
Skipping trades due to hesitation costs money if trades are independent: skipping after every loss costs -$22,536/year (3 trades/day).
Sitting out the next trade after 2 consecutive losses skips ~28% of trading opportunities and costs ~$17,000/year; shutting down the laptop after a loss skips 59% of the year and costs ~$30,000.
The cost is a straight line: approximately -$600 for every 1% of annual trades skipped.
Caveat: If outcomes exhibit positive autocorrelation ('streaky' trader), sitting out breaks even at streakiness >0.08 and becomes profitable above that.

segments.topic: Dash 4: Standing Down After Two Losses
key_points: For a calm trader with no streakiness, standing down after 2 losses costs -$8,442/year.
For a streaky trader, standing down after 2 losses gains +$14,721/year.
Impact varies by trade frequency: at 2 trades/day, the rule is worth $0; at 4 trades/day it breaks even; at 10 trades/day it is worth +$25,303/year.
Volume magnifies the cost or benefit of loss cooldowns.

segments.topic: Dash 5: Take Your Profit and Walk Away (Daily Target)
key_points: Stopping trading once a daily profit target (+2R) is reached costs -$15,314/year for a profitable trader.
This is the only rule where streakiness makes the outcome worse: stopping on a win cuts off positive streaks.
Stopping at a daily target halves total annual profit compared to chasing the target, which only costs ~$3,000 at worst.

segments.topic: Dash 6: Sizing Up After a Hot Streak
key_points: Testing sizing up after 2, 3, or 4 wins in a row, after new account highs, or when up on the day/week/month.
The frequency of triggers ranges from 5% (waiting for 3 wins) to 52% (being up on the month).
The expected monetary value of timing size increases strictly based on win streaks is $0 (within standard error bars).
Winning streaks do not predict future winning probability in independent trade streams.

segments.topic: Dash 7: Be Picky — Fewer vs. Better Trades
key_points: Capping trades per day (e.g. first 1, 2, or 3 of the day) costs between -$466 and -$35,913/year without improving quality.
Grading trade setups and skipping below-median setups produces -$85/year (flat / break-even).
Being excessively selective (taking only the top third or top 17%) reduces annual P&L by -$12,884 and -$28,872 respectively.
However, taking all trades and sizing up to 1.5x on the top half yields +$32,049/year.
Transaction cost sensitivity: if slippage and commissions rise to 0.06R/trade, being picky costs -$12,575 instead of -$85.

segments.topic: Dash 9: Sizing Up on Best Setups
key_points: Cleanest quantitative result in the study: sizing up on top setups consistently outperforms flat sizing.
A trader only needs a +0.62 percentage point win-rate edge on their best setups to justify sizing up at 1.5x.
Break-even win rate spread requirements: 1.25x sizing requires +0.74 pp; 1.50x sizing requires +0.62 pp; 2.00x sizing requires +0.85 pp; 3.00x sizing requires +1.48 pp.

segments.topic: Dash 10: Tail Risk and Capital Protection
key_points: In real markets, stop-losses can experience slippage and black swan gaps (e.g., 1 in 100 trades losing 10x or 20x the intended stop).
At 1% risk per trade with 1 in 100 trades blowing 20x through stop, chance of halving account is 17.1%.
At 2% risk per trade, chance of halving account jumps to 56.2%.
At 5% risk per trade, chance of halving account reaches 99.9%.
The Kelly Criterion suggests ~5% optimal bet for the baseline trader, but Kelly assumes zero gap risk and perfect knowledge of edge.
Universal rules regardless of edge: 93.5% of years have 10-loss streaks; 809 trades needed to measure edge; 99.8% of years experience a 15-loss streak; sizing up on hot streaks is worth -$1,634.
Losing traders benefit from any rule that cuts trade volume (-75% loss reduction from volume reduction).
Profitable traders lose money by skipping trades; they maximize returns by taking setups and sizing up on top reads (capped at 1.5x).
Day traders lose ~75% of profit if daily trade caps prevent executing their full strategy.

segments.topic: Implementation: 4 Claude Prompts for Trade Logs
key_points: Presenter shares 4 prompts to run against exported broker trade history (CSV format) in Claude.
Prompt 1: Streakiness Check (evaluates post-loss win rate vs baseline; needs ~750 trades).
Prompt 2: Replay Rules on History for Day Traders (tests skipping after loss, cooldown after 2 losses, daily loss limit, daily profit target).
Prompt 3: Conviction Audit for Profitable Traders (checks if A+ setup grading win rate spread exceeds 0.6 pp).
Prompt 4: Survival Check (flags trades risking >2% or tail risk >20% account loss).

claims.claim: 93.5% of years contain a run of ten consecutive losses for a trader with a 37% win rate and 2:1 reward-to-risk ratio.
claims.caveats: Assumes 750 trades per year and independent trade probabilities.

claims.claim: A trader needs approximately 809 trades before their measured edge reliably converges near their true edge within a 95% confidence band.
claims.caveats: Derived from binomial distribution confidence interval modeling.

claims.claim: Doubling position size after every loss increases median annual P&L for a profitable trader from $97,830 to $157,834, but increases the probability of halving the account by 2.1 percentage points.
claims.caveats: Requires capping max risk; without a cap, 99.9% of accounts blow up.

claims.claim: Skipping the next trade after two consecutive losses costs a non-streaky profitable trader approximately $17,000 per year.
claims.caveats: Assumes trade outcomes are independent (no streakiness) and the trader takes 3 trades/day on average.

claims.claim: Stopping trading after reaching a daily profit target of +2R costs a profitable trader approximately $15,314 per year.
claims.caveats: Only applies to traders who already possess a positive mathematical expectancy.

claims.claim: Sizing up after a winning streak yields $0 in additional expected value compared to random sizing increases.
claims.caveats: Assumes trade outcomes are statistically independent.

claims.claim: A trader only needs their best setups to win 0.62 percentage points more often than average to profitably size up to 1.5x flat sizing.
claims.caveats: Assumes low transaction costs; costs widen the required spread.

claims.claim: If 1 in 100 trades slips 20x through the stop loss, risking 5% per trade results in a 99.9% probability of losing half the account.

strategies.name: Baseline Profitable Day Trader
strategies.logic: Trade a positive expectancy system consistently across 750 trades per year without discretionary emotion or behavioral intervention.
entry_rules: Take every valid technical/discretionary setup that meets baseline edge criteria (~3 trades/day).
strategies.stated_performance: Median annual ending balance of $97,830 on $50,000 starting account (+$47,830 profit).
strategies.costs_slippage_detail: Evaluated under zero cost as well as 0.02R to 0.06R slippage and commissions per trade.

strategies.name: Asymmetric Conviction Sizing (1.5x on Top Setups)
strategies.logic: Grade setups prior to entry; take all setups flat at 1.0x, but size up to 1.5x on setups graded in the top half of expected quality.
entry_rules: Grade setup prior to entry based on confluence/read quality.
Enter top 50% highest quality setups at 1.5x standard risk.
Enter remaining 50% setups at 1.0x standard risk.
exit_rules: Same as baseline (+2R profit target, -1R stop loss).

strategies.stated_performance: Generates +$32,049 in additional annual P&L compared to flat sizing ($13,720 to $32,049 depending on setup read accuracy).
